old_row.rationale: Job here admits words that wandered untimely; at the conclusion he acknowledges speaking about things he did not understand. The comparison concerns his own assessments of speech, without making every accusation against him true.

findings.finding: The original target Job 42:3 does not expressly confess speaking about things not understood. The author independently noticed this as well and replaced it with Job 40:4-5; the corrected full triple is supported.
findings.resolution: Resolved in the preserved author stage and personally reread as a complete corrected triple.

old_row.relationship: A warning about wrath and God's rebuke of the friends
old_row.rationale: Job warns his opponents about wrath and lawlessness. God's final rebuke of the friends supplies a narrative instance of wrath against their speech; the source's covering wording is retained and no sword is imported.

findings.finding: The final divine response reproves false speech and threatens destruction; it does not explicitly use wrath language. The corrected rationale keeps that distinction.
findings.resolution: Resolved in the preserved author stage and personally reread as a complete corrected triple.

old_row.relationship: The wrongdoer himself and the consequences borne by children
old_row.rationale: Job says possessions fail the sons but asks for repayment to the man himself. Ezekiel expressly distinguishes the son's and father's responsibility; the connection highlights personal recompense without pretending Job's property-loss clause states the same complete legal rule.

findings.finding: Job 21:19 states that He will repay the man himself, rather than merely asking that He do so; the separate wish concerning possessions and sons remains distinct.
findings.resolution: Resolved in the preserved author stage and personally reread as a complete corrected triple.

old_row.relationship: Guarding the commanded way without turning aside
old_row.rationale: Job says he went out in God's commands, guarded His ways and did not turn aside. The psalm likewise connects restrained feet, keeping divine words and not departing from judgments; these are corresponding professions of obedience.

findings.finding: Job 23:11 combines future resolve with past guarding; preserve the actual mixed verb forms.
findings.resolution: Resolved in the preserved author stage and personally reread as a complete corrected triple.

old_row.rationale: Job says he had not known darkness would come and gloom cover his face. His earlier complaint also placed darkness before his face; this repeated image remains a report of experienced distress rather than a confession of hidden crimes.

findings.finding: Gloom covers what lay before the face, rather than the face itself.
findings.resolution: Resolved in the preserved author stage and personally reread as a complete corrected triple.

old_row.relationship: Pledges taken from widows and justice for orphans
old_row.rationale: Job condemns taking an orphan's pack animal and a widow's cow in pledge. Deuteronomy protects orphan and widow justice and forbids a widow's garment as pledge; the different pledged objects remain distinct.

findings.finding: The widow’s cow is taken in pledge; the orphans’ pack animal is led away. Do not extend the pledge clause to both objects.
findings.resolution: Resolved in the preserved author stage and personally reread as a complete corrected triple.

old_row.relationship: Violence against orphans and the law's protection
old_row.rationale: Job describes an orphan snatched from the breast and abuse of the fallen humble. Exodus prohibits mistreating orphans and warns that their cries will bring wrath; the comparison does not invent a debt-enslavement mechanism for the snatching.

findings.finding: Preserve the humbling of one who had fallen rather than importing a distinct humble social class.
findings.resolution: Resolved in the preserved author stage and personally reread as a complete corrected triple.

old_row.relationship: Taking from orphans and the threatened consequence
old_row.rationale: Job connects a dry and failed growth image with goods snatched in an armful from orphans. Exodus warns of judgment for mistreating orphans; the connection preserves the different stated consequences and does not substitute snow or Hades for Job's wording.

findings.finding: The source specifies an armful snatched from orphans without specifying goods.
findings.resolution: Resolved in the preserved author stage and personally reread as a complete corrected triple.

old_row.relationship: Thunder and the limits of human understanding
old_row.rationale: Job calls what is heard of God's ways a mere drop and asks who knows the strength of His thunder. Elihu later joins divine thunder with great works not known to humans; both connect thunder with limited understanding, while remaining distinct speakers.

findings.finding: The source asks who knows when He will act in relation to the strength of His thunder; it does not ask who knows the strength of that thunder.
findings.resolution: Resolved in the preserved author stage and personally reread as a complete corrected triple.
